title: Dates moved back a day
fullTitle: Your Deadline Moved Back a Day. Nobody Edited It.

scenes.narration: Same task, same deadline, two screens. One says January fifteenth. The other says January fourteenth. Nobody edited anything.
captions: Same deadline, two screens: Jan 15 and Jan 14.

scenes.narration: The stored value is a plain string: two thousand twenty-six, oh one, fifteen. A calendar date, with no time of day and no time zone.
captions: A calendar date: no time, no zone.

scenes.narration: Then the code calls new Date on that string. JavaScript reads this date-only form as midnight UTC, so a date quietly becomes a moment. Other string formats are read differently.
captions: Date-only form = UTC midnight. Other formats differ.

scenes.narration: Now format that moment in New York. Midnight UTC is seven in the evening on January fourteenth. In Tokyo it is nine in the morning on the fifteenth, so only some viewers see the bug.
captions: Computed by Intl.DateTimeFormat in this fixture.

scenes.narration: These are two kinds of value. A deadline is a calendar date. A meeting is an instant. Convert instants between zones. Leave dates alone.
captions: Deadline: a calendar date. Meeting: an instant.
Convert instants. Do not convert dates.

scenes.narration: The repair: validate it as a real calendar date, so February thirtieth is rejected, then render year, month and day directly. No conversion. Adding twelve hours is not a fix.
captions: Validate the date, then render it. No Date object.

scenes.narration: The meeting really is an instant: fifteen hundred UTC. Show it in named zones and the clock changes correctly: ten in the morning in New York, and midnight, already January sixteenth, in Tokyo.
Use named zones, not fixed offsets. Future recurring local schedules need zone rules, and daylight saving was kept out of this demo. A date is not always a moment.
captions: Named zones, not fixed offsets. DST not covered here.
A date is not always a moment.
